claim: Start Fable 5.2 at high, the Claude API default, and use your own evals to decide whether to raise or lower effort.
why: High captures most of the capability gain Anthropic describes, with uneven, task-dependent gains above it.
check: Check whether changes from high are supported by evals for the intended workload.
quote: Start at `high`, the default for Claude Fable 5.2 on the Claude API. Depending on the use case, you might move effort up or down, testing against your own evals.

claim: An effort setting tuned on Claude Fable 5.1 or Claude Opus 5.5 should not be carried over to Fable 5.2; the effort sweep should be rerun.
why: Effort levels rank the same across Claude models, but the amount of thinking at each level can differ.
check: If a setup migrated to Fable 5.2 and kept old per-model effort values unchanged, flag it as unvalidated.
quote: So, rerun your effort sweep rather than carrying over a setting you tuned on Claude Fable 5.1 or Claude Opus 5.5.

claim: Low effort suits quick back-and-forth, well-specified tasks, and high-volume workloads such as fast subagents on Fable 5.2.
why: In Anthropic’s coding evaluations, Fable 5.2 at low scored close to Fable 5.1 at higher effort.
check: Subagents doing routine, well-specified work that run at high or xhigh are candidates for low.
quote: `low` suits quick back-and-forth, well-specified tasks, and high-volume workloads (intelligent and fast subagents, for example).

claim: Medium effort fits interactive coding, chat and everyday knowledge work on Fable 5.2, while high fits hard coding, research, agentic work and long unattended runs.
why: High raised scores on most of Anthropic’s tracked coding and knowledge-work evaluations and used more tokens and time than medium.
check: For interactive coding, chat, or everyday knowledge work at high, test whether medium preserves eval results while saving time and tokens.
quote:
* `medium` suits interactive coding, chat, and everyday knowledge work.
* `high` suits hard coding, research, agentic work, and long unattended runs. Turns take noticeably longer to finish than at `medium`.

claim: Anthropic recommends xhigh for Fable 5.2’s hardest long-running coding and agentic work with a measured gain, and max to measure its ceiling or for rare tasks where time and tokens do not matter.
why: In Anthropic’s internal coding evals, xhigh raised scores slightly and used many more tokens, while max takes more time and many more tokens than xhigh.
check: Check for a measured gain on work set to xhigh and a ceiling measurement or unusually cost-insensitive task for work set to max.
quote:
* `xhigh` is for your hardest long-running coding and agentic work where you’ve measured a gain. It raised scores slightly on Anthropic’s internal coding evaluations and used many more tokens.
* `max` is for measuring the model’s ceiling or for the rare task where time and tokens don’t matter.

claim: At max effort, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 run slower and cost more than at xhigh, often for only a small gain.
why: At max the model optimizes for capability without regard to token cost.
check: Check whether max is used to measure the model’s ceiling or on rare tasks where extra time and tokens do not matter.
quote: It runs slower and costs more than at `xhigh`, often for only a small gain.

claim: Fable 5.2 is more likely to end a long, multistep turn early at low or medium effort.
why: Lower effort levels make the model more prone to stopping with a list of what remains, an offer to continue, or at an ordinary obstacle.
check: For agentic work at low or medium, look for avoidable early stops and check whether the prompt tells the model to work through ordinary obstacles.
quote: On long, multistep tasks, Claude Fable 5.2 sometimes ends a turn before the work is done. It might end the turn by listing what’s left to be done, offering to continue, or stopping at an ordinary obstacle such as a timeout. This happens more often at `low` and `medium` effort.

claim: If a Fable 5.2 agent stops early, Anthropic suggests prompt text that tells it to work through ordinary obstacles and respect deliberate blockers.
why: The example addresses unfinished turns and keeps confirmation for risky or destructive actions.
check: When a Fable 5.2 agent stops early, check whether its persistence instructions address ordinary obstacles and protect deliberate blockers.
quote: This prompt tells Claude that ordinary obstacles, such as errors, timeouts, and failing tools, should be diagnosed and worked through. Deliberate blockers, such as a file marked not to be touched, are to be left alone and reported. Treat this as a starting point and adapt the prompt further for your use case.

claim: In Anthropic’s replay of agentic coding sessions at medium effort, a version of the Fable 5.2 persistence prompt roughly halved avoidable unfinished sessions and increased output tokens by about 30 percent.
why: The prompt removed most endings that ask permission or offer to continue, while endings that list remaining work and stop persisted.
check: When testing the prompt on your own workload, measure output tokens and count unfinished turns, including ones that list remaining work.
quote: In testing, Anthropic replayed recorded sessions from an agentic coding product at `medium`. With a version of this text, about half as many sessions ended with unfinished work that could have been continued.

claim: Anthropic recommends keeping an application-side confirmation step for risky or irreversible actions when using the Fable 5.2 persistence prompt.
why: The model asks for confirmation less often with this prompt.
check: Where the persistence prompt is used, check that the setup retains a confirmation step for risky or irreversible actions.
quote: Because the model asks less often with this text, keep your own confirmation step for risky or irreversible actions.

claim: Anthropic recommends naming the exact actions to double-check when writing approval rules for Fable 5.2.
why: In simulated tasks with nobody available to approve, a broad rule about external messages caused Fable 5.2 to hold back about half its routine requests to colleagues and other teams.
check: Look for vague approval categories such as anything outside this conversation in instruction files.
quote: a rule that listed “sending messages to people outside this conversation” among the steps that need approval led the model to hold back about half of its routine requests to colleagues and other teams.

claim: If you want Fable 5.2 to improve code structure as it works, Anthropic suggests telling it that it owns the codebase.
why: On Anthropic’s small coding tasks, the model consolidated duplicated code in under 10 percent of runs without the ownership sentence and about 75 percent with it.
check: For coding agents, check whether ownership is stated consistently with what the user wants (restructure versus minimal change).
quote: You are the owner and long-term maintainer of this codebase, and its design is up to you.

claim: In Anthropic’s small coding tasks, Fable 5.2’s ownership prompt raised output tokens by about 70 to 80 percent and led to unrequested changes.
why: Many unrequested changes were tests and documentation, and some runs changed existing feature behavior.
check: Where the ownership prompt is used, review the diff for unrequested changes and measure its effect on output tokens.
quote: With this prompt, output tokens rose by about 70 to 80 percent and the model made changes nobody had asked for, many of them new tests and documentation.

claim: In Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 tests with the code ownership sentence, an earlier rule against drive-by refactors, renames, or cleanups still left code consolidation in more than half of runs.
why: Anthropic recommends omitting the ownership sentence where the user owns the code and wants minimal changes.
check: Check for the ownership sentence where the user owns the code and wants minimal changes, even if the prompt includes a scope limit.
quote: A rule that limits scope doesn’t cancel it. In Anthropic’s testing, the model still consolidated duplicated code in more than half of runs when “No drive-by refactors, renames or cleanups” appeared earlier in the same prompt.

claim: Anthropic recommends reviewing Fable 5.2 PR summaries alongside the diff after observing that summaries often omitted small changes in its coding tests.
why: A summary alone may miss small changes visible in the diff.
check: Check whether PR reviewers examine both Fable 5.2’s summary and the diff.
quote: A closing PR summary from Claude Fable 5.2 often left out small changes, so review the reported diff and the summary.

claim: With its Fable 5.2 ownership prompt, the migration guide reports code consolidation in about half of small coding trials and about 1.5 times the output tokens.
why: The separate Fable 5.2 prompting guide gives different wording and reports about 75 percent consolidation and 70 to 80 percent more output tokens on its small coding tasks.
check: Check which ownership prompt a setup uses and measure consolidation and output tokens on its own workload.
quote: In testing on small coding tasks it then merged repeated code in about half of the tries (under a tenth without, varying by task), used about 1.5 times the output tokens, and made changes nobody asked for, many of them tests and documentation; the requested feature worked in nearly every try either way.

claim: Fable 5.2 sends progress updates between tool calls as thinking blocks whose text is empty at the default `thinking.display: "omitted"`.
why: A client that renders only text blocks can look silent during a long agentic turn.
check: For clients that should show progress, check for `display: "updates"` with its beta header, or `"summarized"`, and for rendering of non-empty thinking blocks between tool calls.
quote: On Claude Fable 5.2, the updates the model writes between tool calls come back as [progress-update `thinking` blocks](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/thinking#progress-updates). These updates say what the model found and what it’s doing next. Their text is empty at the default `thinking.display` of `"omitted"`.

claim: With Fable 5.2 on platforms that support mid-conversation system messages, a harness can append a turn-scoped reminder after several tool steps with nothing user-readable.
why: In Anthropic’s multi-turn coding tests, this roughly halved the longest silent stretch without a noticeable increase in tokens or time.
check: For silent interactive runs, check whether the harness counts text and non-empty thinking blocks and, if it sends a reminder, retains that message on later requests.
quote: When several pass in a row, you can append this reminder after the latest tool results as a [turn-scoped system message](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/mid-conversation-system-messages#turn-scoped-system-messages) (`clear_at: "next_user_message"`, beta, `mid-conversation-system-clear-at-2026-08-21` header):

claim: A Fable 5.2 prompt asking for an opening line, progress updates, and a closing recap produced a message before the first tool call in every Anthropic coding test run, with roughly 20 percent more output tokens.
why: Anthropic recommends this prompt where a human is directly in the loop.
check: For interactive coding that needs an opening line, check whether the prompt asks for one and measure output tokens if adopting the prompt.
quote: With this text, the model wrote a message before its first tool call in every run of the coding tasks. Note that output tokens per task increased by roughly 20 percent as a result.

claim: When a Fable 5.2 harness cannot append reminders, Anthropic suggests prompting for a one-line update every few tool calls.
why: This prompt cut most long silent stretches in Anthropic’s workflow automation tests.
check: When reminders are unavailable, check for a progress-update instruction and allow for gaps of several tool calls between updates.
quote: Every few tool calls, give the user a one-line update on where things stand.

claim: Anthropic recommends Fable 5.2 for long asynchronous work where nobody needs frequent updates.
why: The model works well on long-running asynchronous tasks but may stay quiet for several tool calls.
check: When routing long Fable 5.2 tasks, check whether users need frequent updates and whether the harness provides them.
quote: Claude Fable 5.2 works well on long-running asynchronous tasks, so Anthropic recommends the model for work where nobody needs frequent updates.

claim: Fable 5.2 delegation depends on the harness and task: in Anthropic’s tests, it rarely delegated on short tasks with a minimal tool and delegated readily in a coding product that invited delegation.
why: Anthropic recommends reviewing existing delegation instructions first when the model starts more subagents than tasks need.
check: Grep system prompts, skills and agent files for lines telling the model to delegate; review them first if subagents are many.
quote: How much Claude Fable 5.2 delegates depends on your harness and tasks. In Anthropic’s testing on short tasks with a minimal subagent tool, it rarely started a subagent. In an agentic coding product whose prompts invite delegation, it delegated readily.

claim: Subagents can be a large part of session cost, so the model each subagent runs on by default should be checked.
why: Delegation can speed up parallel work, and its cost can be a large share of a session.
check: Check which model subagents use by default when reviewing a Fable 5.2 session’s delegation cost.
quote: However, subagents can account for a large part of what a session costs, so check which model your subagents use by default.

claim: If Fable 5.2 delegates more than tasks need, Anthropic recommends explaining subagent cost, when delegation is worthwhile, and how to brief subagents in the tool description.
why: At high effort in Anthropic’s testing, a longer cost-focused description roughly halved subagent counts compared with a shorter version.
check: Review existing delegation prompts first and prioritize testing a revised description where the harness invites delegation and subagents use a large share of tokens.
quote: In the new tool description, state what a subagent adds to the cost of a session, say when delegation is worth it and when it isn’t, and tell the model how to brief a subagent that it starts.

claim: In Anthropic’s agentic coding tests, Fable 5.2 used subagents to review its own work at higher efforts such as xhigh and max, while Fable 5.1 did not on the same tasks.
why: Review can be part of subagent usage at higher effort in a coding harness.
check: When analyzing subagent usage at xhigh or max, check whether the coding harness is spending calls on self-review.
quote: At higher effort levels such as `xhigh` and `max`, Anthropic saw Claude Fable 5.2 use subagents in an agentic coding product to review its own work, which Claude Fable 5.1 didn’t do on the same tasks.

claim: Early testers had good results using Fable 5.2 as planner and orchestrator for other models.
why: Delegation can speed up work that runs well in parallel.
check: For workflows with parallel tasks, consider evaluating Fable 5.2 as planner and orchestrator for other models.
quote: Early testers had good results with Claude Fable 5.2 as the planner and orchestrator for other models.

claim: Cautious notes can accumulate in memory and instruction files and cause Fable 5.2 to ask for unnecessary approval, especially in multi-agent setups in Anthropic’s early testing.
why: Fable 5.2 can keep following obsolete instructions such as never retry.
check: Audit memory files, notes and CLAUDE.md for stale cautions and absolute never rules.
quote: Cautious instructions can build up from past sessions through memory, notes, and instruction files. This can be counterproductive when Claude Fable 5.2 follows the instructions closely and asks for unnecessary approval. In early testing, Anthropic saw this mostly when several agents worked together.

claim: For Fable 5.2, state exceptions to never rules when the model should retain responsibility for the action.
why: The model treats never as absolute.
check: Look for never rules that block an intended action and check whether the instruction states the appropriate exception, such as asking before deletion.
quote: The model treats an instruction that contains “never” as absolute.

claim: When stale cautions make Fable 5.2 ask for unnecessary approvals, Anthropic recommends naming the routine steps it can take on its own.
why: In simulated tasks with existing restrictions, listing retries as permitted raised them from almost none to about half of tries, while a general instruction to act more freely changed nothing.
check: If Fable 5.2 holds routine work, look for vague instructions to act freely and check whether the prompt names the specific steps that need no approval.
quote: With "never" rules, notes and a reviewer's conditions in context, a line at the end of the rules that listed retries among such steps raised them from almost none to about half of the tries; a general instruction to act more freely changed nothing.

claim: Remove or narrow unneeded validation stop conditions that can block autonomous Fable 5.2 work, such as stopping for review at the first error.
why: An unnecessary stop condition can interrupt work that otherwise could continue.
check: Check validation steps and reviewer-agent rules for blanket stop-on-error conditions.
quote: A condition such as “stop and review at the first error” can block autonomous work, so remove or narrow the stopping conditions that you don’t need.

claim: In Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 coding tests at high and xhigh, removing a large token budget from the prompt lowered cost at equivalent performance.
why: The size of a token budget shown in the prompt affects spending, and the tests did not cover the API’s task budgets.
check: Look for harness text that shows remaining tokens to the model and test without it.
quote: In Anthropic’s testing on coding tasks at `high` and `xhigh` effort, removing a large budget lowered cost, with equivalent performance.

claim: At high effort in Anthropic’s tests, Opus 5.5’s “treat that answer as done” lines reduced Fable 5.2’s thinking on follow-ups and made it much less likely to point out earlier mistakes.
why: The lines ask the model to treat the previous answer as settled and focus thinking on the new message.
check: Leave the lines out where self-correction matters and test whether the model still points out its earlier mistakes before adopting them elsewhere.
quote: The model also became far less likely to point out mistakes in its earlier answers.

claim: Fable 5.1 usually followed “answer directly without deliberating,” while that instruction did not stop Fable 5.2 from thinking at medium effort or above in Anthropic’s testing.
why: Fable 5.2 thinks before almost every reply at high and above, even to a greeting.
check: For migrated think-less prompts, check whether the setup uses a lower effort instead of relying on that instruction.
quote: On Claude Fable 5.2, this addition doesn’t stop the model from thinking at `medium` and above. Remove such lines and lower the effort level

claim: Effort has little effect on Fable 5.2 reply length, so Anthropic recommends prompting for the desired length and tone.
why: Effort affects thinking, tool-call volume, turn time, and token use.
check: When a setup uses lower effort to shorten verbose replies, check whether the prompt instead specifies reply length and tone.
quote: Effort has little effect on the length of assistant turn responses. Use prompting to change the length and tone of replies.

claim: Fable 5.2 follows style limits closely, so rules such as one instruction per sentence in 20 words or fewer can make its prose choppy.
why: The model follows writing style rules closely.
check: Look for rigid sentence-length or format limits carried from earlier models and remove those no longer needed.
quote: a hard limit such as “one instruction per sentence, in 20 words or fewer” can make its prose choppy.

claim: For final reports and handoffs Anthropic suggests a Communicating clearly block telling Fable 5.2 to write for a low-context reader who has not seen the tool calls.
why: Readers of final reports after long agentic work usually have not seen the tool calls or files behind them.
check: Where users read handoff messages, check instruction text asks for self-contained reports with key points first.
quote: Write for an intelligent but low-context reader. The person reading has not seen your tool calls, your reasoning or the files you opened, and may be switching in from other work.

claim: Prompts, skills and tool descriptions that ask Fable 5.2 to write out its reasoning in the response should be removed, because they invite reasoning_extraction refusals.
why: The safety classifier declines requests to reproduce internal reasoning in response text; thinking summaries are available instead.
check: Grep instructions for show your reasoning or think step by step in the output.
quote: If your prompts, skills, or tool descriptions ask the model to write out its reasoning in the response, remove those instructions.

claim: Prompt or tool-description changes for Fable 5.2 should be made in new conversations, because editing system or tools in a stored conversation can fail the prefix check with a 400.
why: Thinking blocks are bound to the prefix that produced them.
check: Check whether the harness edits system text, tools, or earlier messages in stored Fable 5.2 conversations and instead use new conversations or append instructions through a supported path.
quote: Make these changes in new conversations only.

claim: The API checks preserved-thinking history on every account for Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, so older accounts can see failures they did not see on Fable 5.1.
why: On the platforms listed in the migration guide, Fable 5.1 enforces the check by default only on accounts created on or after August 31, 2026.
check: For code that builds its own requests, run the migration prefix check before switching, even if the account never saw a mismatch on Fable 5.1.
quote: on Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, the check is enforced for every account, whatever its age

claim: The Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 prefix check requires no migration change if Claude Code, claude.ai, Claude Managed Agents, or the Claude Agent SDK builds the requests.
why: For code that builds its own requests, the source lists conditions covering fixed system and tools, append-only messages, and exact replay of assistant turns.
check: Check which component builds the requests and review prefix handling if the application builds them itself.
quote: Nothing changes for you if Claude Code, claude.ai, [Claude Managed Agents](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/managed-agents/overview), or the [Claude Agent SDK](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/overview) builds your requests.

claim: On the Claude API and Google-managed Claude Models on Google Cloud, switching from Fable 5.2 or Mythos 5.2 to a model outside that pair loses their preserved reasoning for turns run there.
why: The API drops thinking blocks that the receiving model cannot read, and the request succeeds without billing those blocks.
check: Check whether a router or fallback expects earlier thinking blocks to carry over when it switches away from both models.
quote: * **Moving from Claude Fable 5.2 or Claude Mythos 5.2 to any other model** loses their reasoning for the turns that run there. That includes Claude Opus 5.5, Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Mythos 5.1, and Claude Fable 5.2’s fallback models (Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Opus 5).

claim: In the beta API advisor tool, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 executors accept only Fable 5.2 or Mythos 5.2 advisors, and other pairings return HTTP 400.
why: The advisor must be at least as capable as the executor.
check: Check that any advisor paired with a Fable 5.2 or Mythos 5.2 executor uses one of those two model IDs.
quote: A Claude Fable 5.2 or Claude Mythos 5.2 executor accepts only Claude Fable 5.2 or Claude Mythos 5.2 as its advisor. Any other advisor, including Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, returns a 400 `invalid_request_error`.

claim: The Fable 5.2 Messages API returns HTTP 400 for forced tool choice (`any` or `tool`).
why: For schema-valid JSON, the source describes strict tool use with `tool_choice: auto` or JSON outputs, neither of which is available for Fable 5.2 or Mythos 5.2 in CMEK organizations.
check: Look for `tool_choice` set to `any` or `tool` in Fable 5.2 API requests.
quote: Forced tool use isn’t supported.** `tool_choice` set to `{"type": "any"}` or `{"type": "tool", "name": "..."}` returns a 400 `invalid_request_error`.

claim: Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 return HTTP 400 for `computer_20251124` on every platform except Amazon Bedrock, which still accepts that tool.
why: The two models support computer use through `computer_toolset_20260801`.
check: Check for use of the older tool outside Bedrock and for the documented beta header if using it through Bedrock InvokeModel.
quote: A request to either model that declares a `computer_20251124` tool returns a 400 `invalid_request_error` on every platform except Amazon Bedrock.

claim: Fable 5.2’s permitted server-side fallback targets are Opus 4.8 and Opus 5.
why: With `fallbacks: "default"`, the server uses the recommended target for the refusal category when one exists.
check: Check any explicit server-side fallback list for models other than Opus 4.8 or Opus 5.
quote: The permitted fallback targets for Claude Fable 5.2 are Claude Opus 4.8 and Claude Opus 5.

claim: At standard rates, Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 cost $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, down from $10 and $50 on their 5.1 counterparts, with cache reads at $0.20 per million.
why: The migration guide lists the same prices for Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, with standard cache reads at 0.025 times the input rate.
check: Check that standard-rate cost estimates use the correct model version and cache-read rate.
quote: $8 / $40 per MTok input / output (from $10 / $50), 5-minute cache writes $10, 1-hour cache writes $16, cache reads $0.20

claim: For most workloads, Anthropic recommends starting with the latest Opus and moving to Fable 5.2 when higher-effort Opus still falls short on your evals.
why: Fable 5.2 is built for demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work.
check: For workloads routed to Fable 5.2, check whether higher-effort Opus meets the same requirements on the workload’s evals.
quote: and move to Claude Fable 5.2 when your evals on a Claude Opus model at higher effort still don’t meet your requirements.

claim: For Claude models that support effort, tuning it is often a better lever than switching models.
why: Effort trades intelligence for latency and cost inside one model.
check: When weighing a model switch for speed or cost, test whether an effort change on the current model meets the workload’s requirements.
quote: Tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models.

claim: The API default effort is high on Fable 5.2, Fable 5.1, Opus 5 and Sonnet 5.5, but medium on Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5.
why: Defaults differ by model, so a request that omits effort behaves differently across models.
check: When effort is omitted, check whether the selected model’s default matches the workload’s intended effort.
quote: On Claude Fable 5.2, Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5, start with the default (`high`) and adjust up or down based on your evals. On Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5, the default is `medium`; start there and adjust the same way.

claim: Multimodel strategies aim to bill most tokens at a lower rate by having an executor consult a frontier advisor or an orchestrator delegate bulk work to lower-cost workers.
why: The lower-cost model can handle the bulk of the work while the frontier model handles hard decisions or orchestration.
check: Where a frontier model handles all steps, check whether an advisor or delegation pattern would keep most token use on a lower-cost model.
quote: an executor that escalates hard decisions to an advisor, and an orchestrator that delegates bulk work to lower-cost workers.

claim: Anthropic describes Fable 5.2 as its most capable model open to all customers, with Mythos 5.2 offering the same capabilities only to verified organizations.
why: Mythos access depends on Anthropic verification programs.
check: Check that the organization has Anthropic verification before selecting Mythos 5.2.
quote: **Claude Fable 5.2** (`claude-fable-5-2`) is Anthropic’s most capable model open to all customers.

claim: At low effort Haiku 5.5 is more likely to skip a search, stop early or skip a check in long agent prompts.
why: Lower effort reduces thoroughness in long agent prompts.
check: For longer Haiku 5.5 agent tasks at low effort, look for skipped searches, missed checks, or early stops and evaluate the recommended high setting for longer tasks.
quote: In long agent prompts, the model is more likely to skip a search, stop early, or skip a check at `low`.

claim: Effort is a behavioral signal, not a strict token budget, and affects all output tokens including tool calls and thinking.
why: Lower effort also gives fewer and terser tool calls.
check: Do not treat effort as a hard cost cap.
quote: Effort is a behavioral signal, not a strict token budget.

claim: Changing top-level effort between requests can invalidate the prompt cache; vary it across workloads, or use per-message effort on supported models.
why: A top-level effort change can invalidate all or part of the prompt cache.
check: For turns that depend on cache reuse, check for changes to top-level effort and whether per-message effort is supported.
quote: so vary it across workloads rather than within a conversation that relies on cache hits.

claim: On Opus 4.7, raise effort rather than prompting around shallow reasoning on complex problems.
why: Opus 4.7 follows effort levels more strictly than Opus 4.6, especially at low and medium.
check: For shallow reasoning on complex tasks, check for a higher effort setting or targeted prompt guidance when latency requires low effort.
quote: If you observe shallow reasoning on complex problems with Claude Opus 4.7, raise effort rather than prompting around it.

claim: Fable is never the account-type default in Claude Code, so it must be selected explicitly at least once.
why: On most listed plans and providers the account-type default is Opus 5.5, while Microsoft Foundry defaults to Sonnet 4.5.
check: Check the selected model and use the full `claude-fable-5-2` ID for Fable 5.2 in a Claude apps gateway session that serves it.
quote: No Fable model is the account-type default on any plan or provider. Select one explicitly:

claim: In Claude Code, `fable` resolves to Fable 5 in Claude apps gateway sessions and to Fable 5.2 elsewhere unless `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_FABLE_MODEL` overrides it.
why: The alias tracks the Fable version Anthropic currently serves per provider.
check: For a deployment that needs a specific model version, check for the full model ID or a pin through `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_FABLE_MODEL`.
quote: Unless you set `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_FABLE_MODEL`, the `fable` alias resolves to Fable 5 in [Claude apps gateway](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude-apps-gateway) sessions and to Fable 5.2 everywhere else.

claim: The Claude Code account-type default is Opus 5.5 on Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, and Enterprise plans and on the Anthropic API.
why: Organization defaults, an eligible `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL`, a recorded choice, or allowlist enforcement can change what `default` resolves to.
check: If `default` resolves differently, check the organization default, environment variable, recorded model, and allowlist settings.
quote: Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, Enterprise, and Anthropic API**: defaults to Opus 5.5

claim: Claude Code defaults Fable 5.2, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 to medium effort.
why: When Claude Code sends no effort, the API default applies, which is high for Fable 5.2 and Sonnet 5.5 according to the Claude API effort guide.
check: Check `/effort status` to distinguish an effort level sent by Claude Code from `auto`, which leaves the API to choose when no cap requires a level.
quote: Fable 5.2, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 default to `medium`, and Opus 4.7 defaults to `xhigh`.

claim: Claude Code resolves session effort in a fixed order: the CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL variable, then an in-session pick, then --effort, then saved settings, then the model default.
why: An explicit level in `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL` also takes precedence over skill and subagent effort frontmatter.
check: If a session pick or frontmatter effort is not taking effect, check whether `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL` sets a level or uses `auto` or `unset` to request no explicit effort.
quote: Claude Code resolves the session's effort level in this order, taking the first that applies:

claim: Claude Code skill effort overrides session effort through the current turn or the forked run, and subagent effort applies for its run unless the invocation overrides it.
why: An explicit `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL` overrides frontmatter, and user or organization effort caps still apply.
check: If configured skill or subagent effort differs from the effective level, check `context: fork`, invocation settings, the environment variable, and effort caps.
quote: A skill's `effort` applies until the end of the turn it runs in, or for the forked subagent's run with `context: fork`.

claim: A Claude Code subagent or teammate uses the session’s effort pick or `--effort` only if it runs on the main conversation’s model and no other effort level applies.
why: Session effort is calibrated per model, and a level set for the delegated run takes precedence over the session pick.
check: Flag reliance on the session’s effort pick when the agent uses another model or an applicable effort override is set.
quote: On the main conversation's model, a [subagent](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md#choose-an-effort-level) or [teammate](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams.md#specify-teammates-and-models) with [no other level set](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md#when-a-subagent-has-no-effort-field-or-parameter) runs at the level you pick in the session or set with `--effort`.

claim: Claude Code resolves a subagent that inherits the main model to the model in use when the subagent starts.
why: A session model switch also affects subagents started after the switch if they inherit the main conversation’s model.
check: If a custom subagent should stay on a particular model across session switches, check whether its definition sets that model.
quote: If you switch models with `/model`, the switch also reaches [subagents that inherit the main conversation's model](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md#choose-a-model), because Claude Code resolves their model from the one your session is using when Claude starts them.

claim: `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` defaults subagents, teammates, and workflow agents without another model assignment.
why: A per-invocation model or a definition’s `model` field, including `inherit`, takes precedence unless `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE` changes that precedence.
check: When a delegated agent uses an unexpected model, check the environment default, invocation and definition model fields, and the force setting.
quote: A per-invocation model or a definition's `model` field, including `inherit`, takes precedence.

claim: Claude Code switches models in a running session with `/model` and chooses a new session’s model from `--model`, `ANTHROPIC_MODEL`, the `model` setting, or `ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL` in that order.
why: Resumed sessions usually restore the saved model, and the normal priority order applies when an exception prevents restoration.
check: For an unexpected model, check the configuration in priority order and, on resume, verify whether the saved model should have been restored.
quote: You can configure your model in several ways, listed in order of priority:

claim: The Claude Code `opusplan` alias is designed to use `opus` in plan mode and switch to `sonnet` for execution.
why: The pairing uses Opus for planning and Sonnet for implementation, subject to model availability and the allowlist.
check: If `opusplan` stays on Sonnet during planning, check `availableModels` and the provider-specific upgrade rules.
quote:
The `opusplan` model alias provides an automated hybrid approach:

* **In plan mode**: uses `opus` for complex reasoning and architecture decisions
* **In execution mode**: automatically switches to `sonnet` for code generation and implementation

This pairs Opus's reasoning for planning with Sonnet's efficiency for execution.

claim: In Claude Code, `ultrathink` requests deeper reasoning for one turn, while phrases such as “think hard” are passed through as ordinary prompt text.
why: Claude Code adds an in-context instruction and can also raise that turn to xhigh in supported interfaces when the model, provider, and effort caps allow it.
check: Check whether a one-turn effort increase uses `ultrathink` in a supported prompt and shows the rainbow indicator.
quote: Include `ultrathink` anywhere in your prompt to request deeper reasoning on that turn without changing your session effort setting.

claim: Claude Code docs say max effort may show diminishing returns and is prone to overthinking, so it should be tested before broad adoption.
why: Max is meant for hard problems left to run unattended.
check: Check whether broadly configured max effort was evaluated and whether `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL` makes it persist beyond the current session.
quote: `max` may show diminishing returns and is prone to overthinking, so test before adopting it broadly

claim: For Fable in Claude Code, hand it the desired outcome and let it plan, rather than prescribing steps.
why: The docs say Fable sustains long autonomous sessions, investigates before acting, and verifies more often than smaller models.
check: Look for unnecessary step-by-step instructions where describing the outcome would leave Fable room to plan.
quote: hand it the result you want and let it plan the path.

claim: Claude Code describes reminders to test or check as usually unnecessary for Fable because it verifies its own work with less prompting.
why: The Fable 5.1 migration guide gives narrower advice that existing test-before-reporting instructions should be kept when migrating to that model.
check: When reviewing Fable verification reminders, distinguish generic reminders from existing test-before-reporting instructions in a Fable 5.1 migration.
quote: it verifies its own work with less prompting, so reminders to test or check are usually unnecessary.

claim: The Fable 5.1 migration guide tentatively recommends keeping existing test-before-reporting instructions when migrating to Fable 5.1.
why: The migration guide says this rests on a small number of reports and differs from Claude Code’s general Fable guidance that verification reminders are usually unnecessary.
check: When migrating to Fable 5.1, check that existing test-before-reporting instructions were kept even if the setup used the Opus 5 advice to delete verification reminders.
quote: If your existing prompt asks the model to test or check its work before reporting, **keep it** when migrating

claim: You cannot turn thinking off on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 or the Fable models in Claude Code; effort is the lever for how much they think.
why: On those models, `alwaysThinkingEnabled: false` and `MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=0` have no effect, while effort influences how much the model thinks per step.
check: On these Claude Code models, look for configurations that rely on turning thinking off and use effort settings to adjust how much the model thinks.
quote: You can't turn thinking off on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, or the Fable models.

claim: With adaptive reasoning in Claude Code, a prompt or `CLAUDE.md` can ask for more or less frequent thinking within the current effort level.
why: Adaptive reasoning lets the model decide whether to think on each step.
check: If relying on a prompt to suppress thinking, account for the Fable 5.2 prompting guide’s finding that “answer directly without deliberating” did not stop thinking at medium or above.
quote: If you want Claude to think more or less often than the current level produces, you can say so directly in your prompt or in `CLAUDE.md`; the model responds to that guidance within its effort setting.

claim: For main-conversation content fallback in Claude Code, Fable models and Opus 5.5 normally switch to Opus 5 on a biology flag or Opus 4.8 on a cybersecurity flag and continue on that model.
why: Claude Code shows a transcript notice in the main conversation when it switches and uses deployment model IDs on Bedrock, Agent Platform, and Foundry.
check: Check the main transcript for a switch notice and, if no switch occurred, check target resolution and whether `availableModels` excludes the fallback.
quote: biology-flagged requests re-run on Opus 5, and cybersecurity-flagged requests re-run on Opus 4.8.

claim: Content fallback in Claude Code can trigger on the first request because it already includes workspace context, such as CLAUDE.md and git status.
why: Security or biology material in that initial context can trigger a classifier.
check: Use `claude --safe-mode` to test whether customizations triggered an initial fallback, accounting for git status and directory names still being included.
quote: Fallback can trigger on the first request of a session, before you send anything unusual, because the first request carries workspace context such as your CLAUDE.md content and git status.

claim: On third-party providers model versions should be pinned with ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_*_MODEL variables, because aliases resolve to a built-in default that can lag or be unavailable.
why: Without pinning, users may be moved to older models or requests fail.
check: For Bedrock, Agent Platform, Foundry, or Claude Platform on AWS rollouts, check whether the model environment variables pin provider-specific version IDs.
quote: Set the model environment variables to specific version IDs as part of your initial setup.

claim: Anthropic API fast mode offers up to 2.5 times standard speed at higher per-token cost on Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5, with Opus 5 and Opus 4.8 in research preview.
why: Fast mode uses the same model with a speed-oriented API configuration and the same quality and capabilities.
check: Check support, including the November 30, 2026 removal for Opus 4.8, and prefer standard speed for long autonomous tasks where speed matters less, batch or CI/CD, and cost-sensitive work.
quote: Fast mode is a high-speed configuration for supported models, making the model up to 2.5x faster at a higher cost per token.

claim: Claude Code recommends fast mode for interactive work where latency outweighs cost, and standard speed for long autonomous work where speed matters less, batch or CI/CD, and cost-sensitive work.
why: Fast mode trades higher token cost for lower latency, which can help during rapid iteration and live debugging.
check: Review fast mode in pipelines and background sessions against their latency and cost requirements.
quote: Fast mode is best for interactive work where response latency matters more than cost:

claim: The first time fast mode is enabled in a Claude Code conversation, the entire context is charged at the uncached fast input rate.
why: Fast and standard speeds use separate caches, so later switches reread part or all of the conversation uncached.
check: Check when fast mode is enabled and how often speed switches within a long conversation, since enabling it at the start minimizes the first charge.
quote: The first time you enable fast mode in a conversation, you pay the full fast mode uncached input token price for the entire conversation context.

claim: On the Anthropic API, Claude Code’s `fastMode` setting alone has no effect on Fable 5.2 until `/fast` is run while using Fable 5.2.
why: Fast mode on Fable 5.2 persists across sessions only when enabled on that model and per-session opt-in is off.
check: Check whether fast mode was enabled while on Fable 5.2 and whether `fastModePerSessionOptIn` resets it for new sessions.
quote: On Fable 5.2, that setting alone has no effect until you run `/fast` while using Fable 5.2.

claim: On subscription plans fast mode is billed only through usage credits and not covered by plan rate limits.
why: Fast usage draws from credits even if plan usage remains.
check: For subscriptions that use fast mode, check usage-credit spend in the plan’s billing or usage view.
quote: For Claude Code users on subscription plans (Pro/Max/Ultra/Team/Enterprise), fast mode is available via usage credits only and not included in the subscription rate limits.

claim: Setting fastModePerSessionOptIn to true makes every session start with fast mode off, which helps control cost where users run many concurrent sessions.
why: On the Anthropic API, fast mode normally persists for supported models when turned on interactively, with Fable 5.2 requiring opt-in while on that model.
check: If fast mode should start off each session, check that `fastModePerSessionOptIn` is true.
quote: To make every session start with fast mode off, set `fastModePerSessionOptIn` to `true` in any [settings file](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings.md#where-settings-live). Users then enable it with `/fast` in each session.

claim: In Claude Code, the advisor tool fits long multistep tasks with mostly routine turns where plan quality determines the outcome.
why: Claude consults a second, typically stronger model at key moments and sends it the full conversation.
check: When deciding where to use an advisor, check for meaningful decisions to escalate, as short tasks and tasks needing the strongest model every turn gain less.
quote: The advisor fits long, multi-step tasks where most turns are routine but plan quality determines the outcome. Examples include large refactors, debugging sessions where an error keeps recurring, and tasks you want independently checked before Claude declares them done.

claim: In Claude Code the advisor must rank at or above the main model, so a Fable 5.2 main model accepts only a Fable 5.2 advisor.
why: Claude Code ranks models by capability for the advisor role.
check: If the advisor fails to attach, check its rank against the main model and whether an `availableModels` allowlist in the active settings excludes it.
quote:
| Fable 5.2 | Fable 5.2 |

Fable 5.2 requires Claude Code v2.1.321 or later, and

claim: In Claude Code, the model decides when to consult its advisor, and no setting caps or forces these calls.
why: Timing is model-driven rather than rule-based.
check: Check whether the prompt asks for consultations at desired points without assuming it guarantees the resulting call count.
quote: There is no setting to cap or force advisor calls; if you want Claude to consult more or less often during a task, say so in your instructions.

claim: In Claude Code, pairing a faster main model with a stronger advisor typically costs less than using the stronger model throughout.
why: Claude typically calls the advisor at decision points, and each advisor call processes the full conversation anew at the advisor model’s rates.
check: When comparing costs, use the workload’s advisor call frequency and full-transcript reads.
quote: Claude calls the advisor at decision points rather than on every turn, so pairing a faster main model with a stronger advisor typically costs less than running the stronger model throughout.

claim: Subagents inherit the configured advisor and apply the pairing check against their own model.
why: The inherited advisor can be valid for the subagent even when the pairing is invalid for the main model.
check: Check each subagent’s actual model against the configured advisor, regardless of the main model’s pairing.
quote: Subagents inherit the configured advisor and apply the same pairing check against their own model.

claim: When migrating long-running agents to Fable 5.1, Anthropic recommends A/B testing prompts and skills with older step-by-step scaffolding removed.
why: Prompts and skills written for earlier models are often too prescriptive for Fable 5.1 and can reduce output quality.
check: Check whether migration evals compare the old step-by-step scaffolding with prompts that state the goal and constraints.
quote: Prompts and skills written for prior models are often too prescriptive for Claude Fable 5.1 and *reduce* output quality.

claim: Fable 5.1 uses less formatting in chat than earlier models prone to heavy formatting, so Anthropic recommends removing legacy restrictions or saying when formatting is appropriate.
why: The guide describes less bold and fewer headers, lists, and quotation marks in chat.
check: Look for anti-formatting rules carried over from earlier chat models and check whether they still serve the workload.
quote: If the prompt contains anti-formatting language, remove it

claim: In very long sessions, Fable 5.1 can worry about running out of context, most often when the harness shows a remaining-token countdown.
why: It may suggest a new session or trim its own work.
check: Check whether the harness can omit context countdowns or, if they are needed, explicitly tell the model to keep working.
quote: In very long sessions it can worry about running out of context - suggesting a new session or trimming its own work - most often when the harness surfaces a remaining-token countdown.

claim: Fable 5.1 sometimes takes unrequested adjacent actions; the guide recommends stating that when the user is only describing a problem, the deliverable is an assessment and no fix should be applied.
why: Observed examples of unrequested adjacent actions include composing email drafts and creating backup branches.
check: If an agent makes changes on assessment-only requests, check whether its instructions distinguish assessment from implementation.
quote: When the user is describing a problem, asking a question, or thinking out loud rather than requesting a change, the deliverable is your assessment.

claim: For long Fable 5.1 runs, Anthropic recommends requiring each progress claim to be checked against a tool result from the same session.
why: In tests on tasks designed to elicit fabricated status reports, the instruction nearly eliminated them.
check: Check whether the long-run prompt requires a same-session tool result as evidence for each progress claim.
quote: **Ground progress claims on long runs.** Require progress claims to be audited against tool results - in testing this nearly eliminated fabricated status reports on tasks designed to elicit them:

claim: For Fable 5.1, Anthropic recommends delegating frequently with explicit guidance on when to delegate and letting subagents communicate asynchronously.
why: The migration guide says long-lived asynchronous subagents retain context and let the orchestrator keep working while they run.
check: Look for inherited delegation bans or spawn-and-block patterns on work suited to parallel subagents.
quote: Parallel sub-agents are dependable on Claude Fable 5.1 - instead of suppressing delegation (a common prior-model guardrail), use sub-agents frequently and give explicit guidance on *when* delegation is desirable. Sub-agents that communicate **asynchronously** with the orchestrator outperform spawn-and-block:

claim: On a single request for a long deliverable, Fable 5.1 at xhigh or max may draft it in thinking and write it again in the reply, roughly doubling output tokens.
why: Anthropic recommends starting those requests at high and moving up where a quality gain has been measured.
check: For long single-request deliverables at xhigh or max, check for a measured gain and leave room for both thinking and the reply in `max_tokens`.
quote: When one request asks for a long deliverable - a full rewrite of a long document, a large table, a complete code file - it may draft much of it in its thinking and then write it out again as the reply: a longer wait and roughly double the output tokens.

claim: At low effort, Fable 5.1 searches less often and answers from memory more than Fable 5, especially for familiar names of products, models, or tools whose state may have changed.
why: The source suggests raising effort on those turns or prompting the model to verify the name before answering.
check: Look for missed searches on these low-effort turns and evaluate higher effort or a name-verification instruction.
quote: At `low` effort, Claude Fable 5.1 calls a search or retrieval tool less often than Claude Fable 5 and answers from memory more

claim: Fable 5.1 is more likely than Fable 5 to rewrite an entire file when a targeted edit would do.
why: Whole-file rewrites can deliver the same result with more output tokens and time.
check: For unnecessary rewrites on small or medium changes, check whether the prompt or first user message asks for targeted edits.
quote: Claude Fable 5.1 is more likely than Claude Fable 5 to rewrite an entire file where a targeted edit would do - same result, more output tokens and time. Appending this to the system prompt (or the first user message - equally effective) restored targeted edits for small and medium changes:

claim: Compared with Opus 5.5, Fable 5.2 raises default API effort from medium to high and standard prices from $4 input / $20 output to $8 input / $40 output per million tokens.
why: When the request omits effort, Fable 5.2 starts at high while Opus 5.5 starts at medium, so the guide recommends setting effort explicitly.
check: Re-baseline cost and latency when migrating, and test any history edits because Fable 5.2 enforces the prefix check on every account.
quote: the default effort is `high`, not `medium`, so a request that omits `effort` runs one level higher - set it explicitly

claim: At medium effort or above, a Fable 5.2 request that relies on a think-less instruction to fit a small `max_tokens` can hit the limit after a thinking block and before any reply text.
why: Thinking tokens count toward `max_tokens`, and the tested instruction did not stop thinking at medium or above.
check: Check for `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` with no text when a small limit is paired with a think-less instruction, then evaluate a higher limit or lower effort.
quote: A request that relied on such a line to fit a small `max_tokens` can now stop with `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` after a `thinking` block and before any text, because thinking tokens count toward `max_tokens`: raise `max_tokens` or choose a lower effort level.

claim: Cache reads cost 2.5% of base input price on Fable 5.2 and Fable 5.1, 5% on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, and 10% on other Claude models.
why: The cache-read rate is a model-specific fraction of the base input price.
check: Check that cost estimates apply the documented cache-read percentage for the model in use.
quote: prompt cache reads cost 10% of the base input price (2.5% on Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Fable 5.1, 5% on Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5)

claim: Fable 5.2 has a 1M-token context window and a 128K-token synchronous Messages API output limit, with always-on adaptive thinking steered by effort.
why: Thinking cannot be disabled, so effort is the lever.
check: Check whether Fable 5.2 requests assume the documented context and output limits and use effort to tune thinking.
quote: Adaptive thinking lets the model decide how much to think, steered by effort.

claim: Fable 5.2 always uses adaptive thinking and returns HTTP 400 for `thinking.type: disabled` or manual thinking with `budget_tokens`.
why: The model accepts omitted thinking configuration or `thinking.type: adaptive` and uses effort to control thinking depth.
check: Check Fable 5.2 Messages API requests for disabled thinking or manual `budget_tokens` configuration.
quote: Adaptive thinking is always on.** `thinking: {"type": "enabled"}` with `budget_tokens` and `thinking: {"type": "disabled"}` both return a 400 error. Omit `thinking` or send `{"type": "adaptive"}`

claim: In Claude Code, enabling or disabling the advisor mid-session preserves the main model’s prompt cache.
why: Toggling `/advisor` keeps the cached prefix intact, and the advisor’s returned guidance is cached as part of the transcript on later turns.
check: When estimating the effect of toggling the advisor, preserve the main-model cache assumption and account for the advisor reading the full transcript anew on each call.
quote: Enabling or disabling the advisor mid-session does not invalidate your main model's [prompt cache](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching.md). Unlike [switching models](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching.md#switching-models), toggling `/advisor` keeps the cached prefix intact, and the advisor's returned guidance is cached as part of the transcript on later turns.

claim: On the Claude API, Fable 5.2 requires 30-day data retention, so a workspace moving from Opus 5.5 under zero data retention must meet that requirement or confirm eligibility with Anthropic.
why: The migration guide says an organization or workspace that does not meet the retention requirement receives HTTP 400.
check: Before moving an Opus 5.5 workload under zero data retention, check whether the workspace meets the Fable 5.2 retention requirement or has confirmed eligibility with Anthropic.
quote: 30-day data retention is required (an organization running Claude Opus 5.5 under ZDR gets a 400 on every request until a workspace has retention enabled);
